blocks.x: The 2000s were a decade of change, innovation, and discoveries, all of which were reflected in the literature of the era. The transitional period was marked by a shift from playful postmodernism to digitally impacted realism, massive pop culture phenomena, and the radical transformation of the publishing industry. Stories became more grounded in reality and emotion, just as global events, advances in the cognitive sciences, and an increased sense of social fragmentation inspired narratives that reflected the world's social, political, and cultural landscape.

From popular memoirs and other non-fiction books to fictional storytelling that expanded to newer horizons, the 2000s gave rise to some of the most iconic and intense literary works we have seen in the 21st century so far, redefining modern literature as we know it. From globally acclaimed novels like The Kite Runner to YA phenomena like The Hunger Games, here’s our selection of the best books from every year of the 2000s.

1
‘The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier & Clay’ (2000)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/visionquest-trailer-vision-and-ultron-s-existential-odyssey1-500-x-8441-500-x-844-3.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier & Clay

blocks.x: Image via Random House

A historical fiction novel by Michael Chabon, The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier & Clay follows Jewish Czech artist and magician Josef “Joe” Kavalier, who escapes Nazi-occupied Prague and goes to live with his cousin, Sammy Klayman, a writer from Brooklyn. Inspired by Joe’s desire to fight fascism and rescue his family from Europe, he and Sammy create a graphic novel titled The Escapist, featuring a fictional superhero who fights tyranny and oppression, which makes them major figures during the Golden Age of Comics. Several events in the story are taken from the lives of real comic book legends like Jack Kirby and Stan Lee, as well as historical figures like Salvador Dalí and Orson Welles.

At the time of its publication, The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier & Clay was a great success and earned widespread acclaim, winning the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. The novel is a brilliant blend of high-concept literature and pop-culture history, and finely captures the actual Golden Age of comics through heavy human themes. The novel ranks among the greatest works of contemporary American fiction and is an early masterpiece of the 21st century.

2
‘Atonement’ (2001)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress%2Fwp-content%2Fauthors%2F652e35569bbcc-WhatsApp%20Image%202023-10-17%20at%2012.47.07%20PM.jpeg?fit=crop&w=90&h=90
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/atonement-book-cover0.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
Image via Jonathan Cape

A British novel by Ian McEwan, Atonement follows the decades-spanning tragedy of a young girl whose innocent mistake leads to lifelong consequences. Set in England and France across three time periods — 1935, WWII, and the present day — the story follows a 13-year-old Briony Tallis, an aspiring writer, whose misinterpretation of a grave incident ruins several lives and tears her family apart, impacting her adulthood and the kind of author she becomes. The novel was later adapted into a 2007 film starring Saoirse Ronan as Briony Tallis.

Atonement is noted for its shifting narrative of family drama that transitions into a profound meditation on guilt, memory, and the ethical power of storytelling. Published in 2001, Atonement was shortlisted for the year’s Booker Prize for Fiction and won the 2002 National Book Critics Circle Award for Fiction. The novel has since been widely considered one of McEwan’s best works and a masterpiece of modern literature.

3
‘Middlesex’ (2002)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/visionquest-trailer-vision-and-ultron-s-existential-odyssey1-500-x-8441-500-x-844-4.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
Image via Farrar, Straus and Giroux

A Pulitzer Prize–winning novel by Jeffrey Eugenides, Middlesex follows the story of the narrator and protagonist, Cal Stephanides, an intersex Greek man born with a genetic mutation. The book reveals the effect his gender identity has on three generations of his family and the phenomenal changes it brings to his life. The story explores themes of ethnic identity, immigrant experiences, gender identity, rebirth, and the American dream. The novel also has many allusions to Greek mythology, derived from Eugenides' observations of his Greek heritage.

Middlesex is a richly detailed family saga across three timelines, but it is essentially a very heartfelt coming-of-age story of a young person. Despite its heavy themes, it is a high-spirited, positive story about nature versus nurture, social constructs versus reality, and what it truly means to be reborn. When it was published, Middlesex met with immense critical acclaim and accolades, ranking at number one on several prestigious bestseller lists, and is generally regarded as one of the best novels of 2002.

4
‘The Kite Runner’ (2003)

Hailed as one of the most powerful literary works of this century, Afghan-American author Khaled Hosseini’s debut novel, The Kite Runner, is a deeply moving story of two young boys, Amir and Hassan, who grow up during the Afghan conflicts of the 1970s and the rise of the Taliban regime. As they navigate childhood and adolescence amid turbulent times, Amir and Hassan become close friends, but when an act of transgression breaks that bond, Amir sets out to atone for his sins in the years to follow. The novel was adapted into a film by Marc Forster in 2007.

The Kite Runner was not an instant success but eventually grew into a global literary icon of its time, and was widely praised for its themes and touching narrative on childhood trauma, lifelong guilt, and loyalty. Heartbreaking and hopeful at the same time, the story serves as a powerful, raw window into the social and political history of Afghanistan, told through the tragic transformation of friendship between two young boys. Translated into over 40 languages since its first publication, The Kite Runner ranks among the most popular and acclaimed books of the last 26 years.

5
‘Gilead’ (2004)

Written by Marilynne Robinson, Gilead is an epistolary novel chronicling the fictional autobiography of John Ames, an elderly white Congregationalist pastor in the small, secluded titular town in Iowa. Realizing his death is imminent, Ames writes an account of his life to his seven-year-old son, narrating his past, faith, and the history of his family through a series of letters. The first of a tetralogy, Gilead is followed by three subsequent novels, Home, Lila, and Jack, which also use events and characters from the first book.

Gilead was ranked as a bestseller by various prestigious publications and has earned a place on BBC News’ list of the 100 most influential novels. The story serves as a deep exploration of faith and doubt and has since been a subject of debate on Christian multiculturalism in literature. Emotionally honest and deeply spiritual, while also being suspenseful, Gilead is widely considered a masterwork of modern American literature and a deeply rewarding read.

6
‘Never Let Me Go’ (2005)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/never-let-me-go.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: The book cover for Never Let Me Go by Kazuo Ishiguro

blocks.x: Image via Vintage Books

Written by Nobel Prize winner Kazuo Ishiguro, one of the most critically acclaimed contemporary fiction authors in the English language, the sci-fi novel Never Let Me Go is set in an alternative 1990s England at an elite boarding school. The story revolves around Kathy, Ruth, and Tommy, who reflect on their heavily sheltered childhood and their inevitable future. The book was adapted into a 2010 film by Mark Romanek, starring Carey Mulligan as Kathy, Andrew Garfield as Tommy, and Keira Knightley as Ruth.

Never Let Me Go begins as a coming-of-age novel but quickly turns into a dark, dystopian story about friendship, love, memory, and what it truly means to be human. The book is tender and thoughtful, but also devastating and horrifying at the same time, and subliminally so. Though it did not win any awards, Never Let Me Go was shortlisted for the Booker Prize, the Arthur C. Clarke Award, and the National Book Critics Circle Awards, and has since ranked among the greatest sci-fi novels of the last five decades.

7
‘Eat, Pray, Love’ (2006)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/eat-pray-love-julia-roberts.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Julia Roberts in Eat, Pray, Love smiling and looking at the sky.

blocks.x: Image via Columbia Pictures

A memoir by American author Elizabeth Gilbert, Eat, Pray, Love: One Woman's Search for Everything Across Italy, India and Indonesia, is a chronicle of Gilbert’s personal experiences traveling around the world after a difficult divorce. In Italy, she finds gastronomic enjoyment; in India, she finds spirituality, and in Bali, she finds love. The book is structured in three distinct sections, mirroring the three parts of its title, each narrating what she discovered on her journeys.

Eat, Pray, Love is exactly what it says in its title — one woman’s search for everything and herself, and how that journey shapes her life. Gilbert shares a heartfelt and inspiring story of forgiveness, finding balance, and discovering love and joy in the most unexpected places, with wit, intelligence, and vivid details. When it was first published, Eat, Pray, Love remained a New York Times Bestseller for months and was discussed extensively on The Oprah Winfrey Show, later getting adapted into a film with Julia Roberts portraying Elisabeth Gilbert.

8
‘Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows’ (2007)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/harry-potter-and-the-deathly-hallows-2007-book-cover.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows - 2007 - book cover

blocks.x: Image via Bloomsbury
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2024/12/amazon01_logo-1.jpg?q=49&fit=contain&w=75&h=75&dpr=2

The final book of J.K. Rowling’s Harry Potter series, Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows, sees Harry, Ron, and Hermione set out on a quest to find and destroy the last of Lord Voldemort’s Horcruxes, in order to finally destroy the Dark Lord. Their efforts are complicated by the open takeover of the magical world by Voldemort and his acolytes, with even Hogwarts falling under their control. Simultaneously, Harry learns of the legendary Deathly Hallows, artefacts that allegedly give their bearer power over death itself, and the late Professor Dumbledore’s personal connection to them.

The release of Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows was a global cultural moment, with months of anticipation culminating in one of the biggest book releases of all time. Release parties and signings may be commonplace for fantasy novels these days, but none of those compare to the universal celebration the book’s arrival inspired in its global fanbase, with the novel holding a Guinness World Record for most novels sold within 24 hours of release. It’s a masterfully written conclusion to the seven-book saga that wraps up Harry’s story in a satisfying way, with many moments that are sure to bring readers to tears.

9
‘The Hunger Games’ (2008)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/untitled-design-29.png?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
Image via Scholastic Press

A dystopian young adult novel by Suzanne Collins, The Hunger Games is set in the future post-apocalyptic nation of Panem in North America and is narrated by a 16-year-old girl named Katniss, who takes her sister’s place in the titular annual event, which was created as a punishment for a past failed rebellion against the Capitol. In the event, one boy and one girl between the ages of 12 and 18 are chosen from the 12 impoverished districts of the nation to compete in a televised battle royale. The novel is the first in The Hunger Games Trilogy, followed by Catching Fire and Mockingjay.

When it was first published in 2008, The Hunger Games was an instant bestseller and a critical success, earning rave reviews for its plot, setting, and character development, as well as its surprising political commentary. The book draws elements from Greek mythology, Roman history, global political conflicts, and contemporary reality television tropes. Widely considered one of the most influential works in YA fiction, The Hunger Games has since remained a benchmark for the genre and an important pop culture icon, extending its impact on cinema with the launch of the film franchise.

10
‘The Lost Symbol’ (2009)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/assets/images/sr-db-logo-icon-colored-dark.svg?v=1.9
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/the-lost-symbol-peacock-social-featured.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
Image via Peacock

A mystery thriller by Dan Brown featuring Harvard University professor and symbologist Robert Langdon, The Lost Symbol follows Langdon as he attempts to rescue his mentor and longtime friend, Peter Solomon, who is kidnapped. In exchange for Peter’s return, the kidnappers force Langdon to unlock an ancient Masonic pyramid and find a "lost word" that supposedly grants god-like power. The Lost Symbol marks the third book in Brown’s Robert Langdon novel series after Angels & Demons and The Da Vinci Code.

Fast-paced and absolutely unputdownable, The Lost Symbol is another fantastically puzzling maze created by Brown. Just like his other books in the series, The Lost Symbol successfully connects the sacred with the secular, the ancient with the modern, and strange facts with historical fiction. Even though the book did not become as globally renowned as The Da Vinci Code or Angels & Demons and did not win any awards, The Lost Symbol was a massive success, becoming the fastest-selling adult novel in history and selling a million copies in its first print edition alone.

‘The Kite Runner’ (2003)

Hailed as one of the most powerful literary works of this century, Afghan-American author Khaled Hosseini’s debut novel, The Kite Runner, is a deeply moving story of two young boys, Amir and Hassan, who grow up during the Afghan conflicts of the 1970s and the rise of the Taliban regime. As they navigate childhood and adolescence amid turbulent times, Amir and Hassan become close friends, but when an act of transgression breaks that bond, Amir sets out to atone for his sins in the years to follow. The novel was adapted into a film by Marc Forster in 2007.

The Kite Runner was not an instant success but eventually grew into a global literary icon of its time, and was widely praised for its themes and touching narrative on childhood trauma, lifelong guilt, and loyalty. Heartbreaking and hopeful at the same time, the story serves as a powerful, raw window into the social and political history of Afghanistan, told through the tragic transformation of friendship between two young boys. Translated into over 40 languages since its first publication, The Kite Runner ranks among the most popular and acclaimed books of the last 26 years.

‘Gilead’ (2004)

Written by Marilynne Robinson, Gilead is an epistolary novel chronicling the fictional autobiography of John Ames, an elderly white Congregationalist pastor in the small, secluded titular town in Iowa. Realizing his death is imminent, Ames writes an account of his life to his seven-year-old son, narrating his past, faith, and the history of his family through a series of letters. The first of a tetralogy, Gilead is followed by three subsequent novels, Home, Lila, and Jack, which also use events and characters from the first book.

Gilead was ranked as a bestseller by various prestigious publications and has earned a place on BBC News’ list of the 100 most influential novels. The story serves as a deep exploration of faith and doubt and has since been a subject of debate on Christian multiculturalism in literature. Emotionally honest and deeply spiritual, while also being suspenseful, Gilead is widely considered a masterwork of modern American literature and a deeply rewarding read.

‘Never Let Me Go’ (2005)

Image via Vintage Books

Written by Nobel Prize winner Kazuo Ishiguro, one of the most critically acclaimed contemporary fiction authors in the English language, the sci-fi novel Never Let Me Go is set in an alternative 1990s England at an elite boarding school. The story revolves around Kathy, Ruth, and Tommy, who reflect on their heavily sheltered childhood and their inevitable future. The book was adapted into a 2010 film by Mark Romanek, starring Carey Mulligan as Kathy, Andrew Garfield as Tommy, and Keira Knightley as Ruth.

Never Let Me Go begins as a coming-of-age novel but quickly turns into a dark, dystopian story about friendship, love, memory, and what it truly means to be human. The book is tender and thoughtful, but also devastating and horrifying at the same time, and subliminally so. Though it did not win any awards, Never Let Me Go was shortlisted for the Booker Prize, the Arthur C. Clarke Award, and the National Book Critics Circle Awards, and has since ranked among the greatest sci-fi novels of the last five decades.

7
‘Eat, Pray, Love’ (2006)

Image via Columbia Pictures

A memoir by American author Elizabeth Gilbert, Eat, Pray, Love: One Woman's Search for Everything Across Italy, India and Indonesia, is a chronicle of Gilbert’s personal experiences traveling around the world after a difficult divorce. In Italy, she finds gastronomic enjoyment; in India, she finds spirituality, and in Bali, she finds love. The book is structured in three distinct sections, mirroring the three parts of its title, each narrating what she discovered on her journeys.

Eat, Pray, Love is exactly what it says in its title — one woman’s search for everything and herself, and how that journey shapes her life. Gilbert shares a heartfelt and inspiring story of forgiveness, finding balance, and discovering love and joy in the most unexpected places, with wit, intelligence, and vivid details. When it was first published, Eat, Pray, Love remained a New York Times Bestseller for months and was discussed extensively on The Oprah Winfrey Show, later getting adapted into a film with Julia Roberts portraying Elisabeth Gilbert.

8
‘Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows’ (2007)

Image via Bloomsbury

The final book of J.K. Rowling’s Harry Potter series, Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows, sees Harry, Ron, and Hermione set out on a quest to find and destroy the last of Lord Voldemort’s Horcruxes, in order to finally destroy the Dark Lord. Their efforts are complicated by the open takeover of the magical world by Voldemort and his acolytes, with even Hogwarts falling under their control. Simultaneously, Harry learns of the legendary Deathly Hallows, artefacts that allegedly give their bearer power over death itself, and the late Professor Dumbledore’s personal connection to them.

The release of Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows was a global cultural moment, with months of anticipation culminating in one of the biggest book releases of all time. Release parties and signings may be commonplace for fantasy novels these days, but none of those compare to the universal celebration the book’s arrival inspired in its global fanbase, with the novel holding a Guinness World Record for most novels sold within 24 hours of release. It’s a masterfully written conclusion to the seven-book saga that wraps up Harry’s story in a satisfying way, with many moments that are sure to bring readers to tears.

‘The Hunger Games’ (2008)

Image via Scholastic Press

A dystopian young adult novel by Suzanne Collins, The Hunger Games is set in the future post-apocalyptic nation of Panem in North America and is narrated by a 16-year-old girl named Katniss, who takes her sister’s place in the titular annual event, which was created as a punishment for a past failed rebellion against the Capitol. In the event, one boy and one girl between the ages of 12 and 18 are chosen from the 12 impoverished districts of the nation to compete in a televised battle royale. The novel is the first in The Hunger Games Trilogy, followed by Catching Fire and Mockingjay.

When it was first published in 2008, The Hunger Games was an instant bestseller and a critical success, earning rave reviews for its plot, setting, and character development, as well as its surprising political commentary. The book draws elements from Greek mythology, Roman history, global political conflicts, and contemporary reality television tropes. Widely considered one of the most influential works in YA fiction, The Hunger Games has since remained a benchmark for the genre and an important pop culture icon, extending its impact on cinema with the launch of the film franchise.

10
‘The Lost Symbol’ (2009)

Image via Peacock

A mystery thriller by Dan Brown featuring Harvard University professor and symbologist Robert Langdon, The Lost Symbol follows Langdon as he attempts to rescue his mentor and longtime friend, Peter Solomon, who is kidnapped. In exchange for Peter’s return, the kidnappers force Langdon to unlock an ancient Masonic pyramid and find a "lost word" that supposedly grants god-like power. The Lost Symbol marks the third book in Brown’s Robert Langdon novel series after Angels & Demons and The Da Vinci Code.

Fast-paced and absolutely unputdownable, The Lost Symbol is another fantastically puzzling maze created by Brown. Just like his other books in the series, The Lost Symbol successfully connects the sacred with the secular, the ancient with the modern, and strange facts with historical fiction. Even though the book did not become as globally renowned as The Da Vinci Code or Angels & Demons and did not win any awards, The Lost Symbol was a massive success, becoming the fastest-selling adult novel in history and selling a million copies in its first print edition alone.
